title.en: The Four Tulans and the Obsidian Stone's Creation
title.zh: 四圖蘭與黑曜石之造人

region.en: Tulan (mythic place of origin), symbolic pin on the Pacific slope of Chiapas-Guatemala
region.zh: 圖蘭（神話起源地），以恰帕斯-危地馬拉太平洋坡地為象徵定位

texts.period: Cakchiquel annals compiled 1571-1604 by Xahila family; Brinton translation 1885

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels (Memorial de Tecpan Atitlan), trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 4-5

summary.en: Gagavitz and Zactecauh teach that there are four Tulans — at sunrise, at Xibalbay, at sunset, and where God is — and that man was first made in misery by the Maker and Creator, sustained by the Obsidian Stone, until the coyote, crow, and Tiuh Tiuh brought maize from Paxil and human flesh was kneaded into being.
summary.zh: 加加維茨與扎克特考教示：圖蘭有四——日出處、希巴爾巴、日落處與神之所在。人初受造於苦難，由塑造者所造、以黑曜石為支柱，直至郊狼、鴉與蒂烏·蒂烏自帕希爾帶來玉米，人之肉身方由玉米揉成。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase/summary of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Four men came from Tulan: there is one Tulan at the sunrise, one at Xibalbay, one at the sunset — from this one at the sunset we came, from Tulan beyond the sea — and one is where God is. Therefore there are four Tulans, and it was at Tulan that, arriving, we were brought forth and begotten by our mothers and our fathers.
passages.note: Quoted and lightly condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 4; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then the Obsidian Stone is brought forth by the precious Xibalbay, and man is made by the Maker, the Creator; the Obsidian Stone was his sustainer when man was made in misery. He was fed with wood and leaves; he wished only the earth; he could not speak, could not walk; he had no blood, he had no flesh.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 5; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Nothing was found to feed him, until two brutes knew there was food in the place called Paxil: the Coyote and the Crow. The Coyote, killed by the brute Tiuh Tiuh as he gathered maize, yielded the grain for kneading, and the blood of the serpent and the tapir was brought from within the sea to mix the maize. Of it the flesh of man was formed — thirteen men and fourteen women, who talked, walked, had blood, had flesh, and married.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 5; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Tribute at the Gate of Tulan and the Idols of Wood and Stone
title.zh: 圖蘭門口的貢賦與木石之像

region.en: Tulan (mythic place of origin), symbolic pin on the Pacific slope of Chiapas-Guatemala
region.zh: 圖蘭（神話起源地），以恰帕斯-危地馬拉太平洋坡地為象徵定位

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 6-8

summary.en: Thirteen divisions and seven tribes gather at Tulan in darkness and pay tribute in jade, silver, featherwork, painted and sculpted wares, calendars, and songs. The Obsidian Stone assigns them their burdens, and as they descend they are given 'the wood and stone which deceive' — the idols that will travel with them.
summary.zh: 十三部與七族於黑暗中聚於圖蘭，奉納玉、銀、羽飾、雕繪之物、曆法與歌。黑曜石為其定下重負；下行之際，獲授「欺騙的木與石」——即將隨行的神像。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: We were ordered to come by our mothers and fathers, we the thirteen divisions and the seven tribes, and we came to Tulan in the darkness and the night. There we gave our tribute: jade and silver, green feathers worked and sewed, articles painted and sculptured, flutes, songs, astrological calendars and reckoning calendars, fine and common cacao — only such riches were paid in Tulan.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 6; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then the Obsidian Stone spoke: 'You, my sons, my daughters, these are your burdens which you shall sustain. There are your hills and plains, beyond the ocean; there it is that you shall lift up your faces. These are the burdens I shall give you, your riches, your majesty.' And as they descended from Tulan and Xibalbay they were given the wood and stone which deceive — the idols that would stand in their houses.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 7; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Portent Birds at the Gate

region.en: Tulan (mythic place of origin), symbolic pin on the Pacific slope of Chiapas-Guatemala
region.zh: 圖蘭（神話起源地），以恰帕斯-危地馬拉太平洋坡地為象徵定位

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 13-14

summary.en: As the tribes go forth from Tulan, three birds cry their omens: the 'guard of the ravine' predicts death, the owl claims to be their portent, and the parroquet wails from the sky. The migrants answer each bird in its turn, refusing fear and reading the parrot as merely the sign of spring.
summary.zh: 諸族自圖蘭啟程之際，三隻鳥相繼啼兆：「谷之守衛」預言死亡；鴞自稱其兆；鸚鵡於空中哀鳴。遷徙者逐鳥回應，拒斥恐懼，並謂鸚鵡僅是春天的信號。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: A bird called the guard of the ravine began to complain within the gate of Tulan as we went forth: 'You shall die, you shall be lost, I am your portent. Do you not believe me? Truly your state shall be a sad one,' said this brute to us.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 13; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then the owl, seated on a red tree, complained: 'I am your portent.' 'You are not our portent, although you would like to be,' we answered it. And the parroquet cried from the sky: 'I am your portent; you shall die.' But we said: 'Do not speak thus; you are but the sign of spring; you wail first when it is spring, and when the rain ceases you wail.'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 14; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Staff of the Red Tree: Crossing the Sea

region.en: The sea crossing from Tulan, symbolic pin on the Gulf of Tehuantepec coast
region.zh: 自圖蘭渡海，以特萬特佩克灣岸為象徵定位

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 15-16

summary.en: At the sea all the warriors of the seven villages despair — no one has ever crossed. Gagavitz and Zactecauh plant the root of the red staff they carried from Tulan in the sand, and the sea parts from the sand, uncovering a road above and below the water. All pass over and rejoice: the staff, not a boat, is the vessel of the migration.
summary.zh: 抵海之際，七村戰士皆絕望——從無人渡此海。加加維茨與扎克特考將自圖蘭攜來的紅杖之根植入沙中，海水與沙分離，露出水上水下之道。眾人相繼渡海而喜：杖而非舟，是遷徙的舟楫。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: There were gathered together the warriors of all the seven villages at the sea, and a great number perished, devoured by sorrow. 'There is no means of passing, nor is it told of anyone who has passed the sea,' they said. 'In thee alone, my brother, in thee alone have we hope.'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 15; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then there was a red tree, our staff, which we had taken in passing from the gate of Tulan — and therefore we are called the Cakchiquel people. The root of this staff was pushed into the sand of the sea, and soon the sea was separated from the sand; the sand became as a line and grew wide above the sea and below the sea, and we passed out. Then all rejoiced when they saw sand in the sea.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 16; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: War with the Nonoualcats: Names Drawn from Salvation
title.zh: 與諾諾瓦爾卡特之戰：由救法取名

region.en: Zuyva (mythic eastern city), symbolic pin on the Pacific coastal plain of Guatemala
region.zh: 祖伊瓦（東方神話之城），以危地馬拉太平洋岸平原為象徵定位

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 19-20

summary.en: The migrants meet the Nonoualcats in their boats on the ocean border, rout them, and seize the boats to cross; but entering the great town of Zuyva in the east, they meet sorcery — fighting in the houses, with dogs and wasps, attackers ascending into the air — and are driven back. Each nation then names itself by its salvation: Tohohil in the sky, Cakix in the ara's mouth, Gucumatz in the water, Akalahay in the honeycomb.
summary.zh: 遷徙者於海際遭逢乘舟的諾諾瓦爾卡特人，擊潰之並奪舟渡海；然而入東方大城祖伊瓦，遭遇妖術——屋內搏鬥、與犬蜂作戰、敵人升空——而被逐回。諸族遂各以其救法命名：托霍希爾在天、卡基希在鸚鵡之口、庫庫馬茲在水、阿卡拉哈伊在蜂巢。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Soon we met face to face a party of warriors called those of Nonovalcat and those of Xulpit, on the border of the ocean, in their boats. The fighting was fearful; they were routed by us, half the fighting being in the boats, and we entered the boats of those of Nonovalcat to cross the sea while our battle was not yet known.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 20; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Truly it was fearful in the town and houses of those of Zuyva, there in the east: the noise was great, the dust oppressive; fighting went on in the houses, fighting with the dogs, the wasps — for they were in the air and in the earth, ascending and descending everywhere against us, and thus they showed their magic and sorcery. We were routed, and all the warriors returned each one by himself to Tapcu Oloman, gathering in sadness.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 20; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: When we asked each other where our salvation was, each nation named it and took its name: the Quiche men said their salvation was in the sky, and were called Tohohil; the Zotzil said it was in the mouth of an ara, and were called Cakix; we said it was in the middle of the valley, entering the earth, and were called Chitagah; another said it was in the water and was called Gucumatz; and the Akahals, who said they might be saved in a honeycomb, were called Akalahay. Do not believe that many were saved: the Evil One scattered us abroad.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 20; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Zakiqoxol, the Heart of the Forest

region.en: Forests between Chiyol and Hunahpu, Guatemalan highlands
region.zh: 危地馬拉高地奇奧爾與烏納普之間的森林

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 21-22

summary.en: Passing between the mountain ranges, the migrants meet a fire built on the road by Zakiqoxol, the spirit of the forest, who kills many men. Challenged as a hideous guardian, he begs for clothes, and they dress him in his blood-red cuirass and shoes; thus clothed and named, he spares them and sinks back into the woods.
summary.zh: 穿越山脊之間，遷徙者遇見扎基科紹爾——森林之靈、殺人甚多的凶神——在路旁所燃之火。眾人斥其為醜陋的守路者，他求衣蔽體；他們便為他穿上血紅胸甲與血紅鞋履；穿著命名之後，他放過他們，隱回林中。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: Twice they turned their steps and passed between the mountain ranges to the fire, to Hunahpu; and there they met face to face in the spirit of the forest the fire called Zakiqoxol. Truly, this Zakiqoxol kills many men; truly he is fearful, a robber, they say.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 21; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Going on, they arrived in the middle of the woods at a fire built by one guarding the road. 'Who are these boys whom we see?' said he. And they sent forward the Qoxahil and the Qobakil with their mysterious vision, and they said: 'Who are you? We shall kill you. Why do you guard the road here?'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 22; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then he said: 'Do not kill me; I, who am here, I am the heart of the forest.' And he asked that he might clothe himself, and they gave him wherewith to clothe himself: a change of garment, his blood-red cuirass, his blood-red shoes, the dying raiment of Zakiqoxol. By this means he saved himself, descending into the forest, and the trees and birds murmured where he had been — the place called Chitabal, the Place of Disquiet.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 22; not verbatim throughout.

region.en: Mem and Tacna (mythic stations of the migration), Guatemalan highlands
region.zh: 梅姆與塔克納（遷徙途程），危地馬拉高地

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, sec. 24

summary.en: Among the peoples of Mem and Tacna the migrants cannot make themselves understood — hence the name Mem, the mute. The people are kind and beg them to stay, wishing them to forget their own speech; but their heart is 'as a stone', and they hold to their tongue and move on.
summary.zh: 在梅姆與塔克納的人們中，遷徙者無法使己意被解——故名梅姆，即啞。其人雖善，懇請他們留下，望其忘卻己語；但其心如石，遂守其舌，前行而去。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: They went to the places, Meme and Tacna, for the second time. They could not speak well, hence the name Mem. Truly, they were good people. They spoke to mock us, and we remained to learn their language.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 24; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: They said to us: 'Thou our lord, remain with us; we are thy elder and younger brother; abide with us.' They wished us to forget our speech, but our heart was as a stone when we arrived with them, and we went on with our words and our days intact.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 24; not verbatim throughout.

region.en: Carchah (mythic station of the migration), Guatemalan highlands
region.zh: 卡爾恰（遷徙途程），危地馬拉高地

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, sec. 25

summary.en: At Carchah the migrants come before Nacxit, a great lord, whose vassals guard his sovereignty. They are told to bow beneath a carved stone threshold in his house to receive majesty and the Panther Seat; some obey and receive sovereignty, others refuse the stone and receive nothing.
summary.zh: 在卡爾恰，遷徙者來到偉大的君王納克希特面前，其封臣守衛其王權。眾被告知：須俯身於其屋中雕琢的石門檻之下，方可獲得威儀與豹座；有人從之而得王權，有人拒石而一無所獲。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: They passed over with the sons of Valil and the sons of Tzunun; they went forth from Merac and Nacxit. Truly this Nacxit was a great lord, and the vassals who aided him to seize the sovereignty were assembled there.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 25; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: It was beautiful to see all the warriors there, and Nacxit spoke to them: 'Bow beneath the carved stone threshold of my house, and I will give you your majesty, your canopy, your royal seat.' Then the warriors consulted among themselves; some bowed beneath the stone, and to them sovereignty was given, and they came forth crowned with the power of Nacxit.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 25; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Gagavitz Captures the Heart of the Mountain

region.zh: 加克紹爾火山（富埃戈火山），危地馬拉高地

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 31-32

summary.en: The volcano Gagxanul burns for a whole year, and no one can pass. Gagavitz and Zakitzunun put aside bow and shield, dig a trench, set water and green grass against the fire, and Gagavitz descends head-first into the mountain. He reappears terrible with the fire subdued — 'he died, and yet he has come down' — and the dance of the Heart of the Mountain is founded.
summary.zh: 加克紹爾火山整整燃燒一年，無人能過。加加維茨與扎基特蘇放下弓盾，掘壕引水、以青草敵火，加加維茨頭先探入山體。他再現時面目可怖而火已馴服——「他死了，卻又走出來」——「山之心」之舞由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: They saw the fire of the mountain called Gagxanul; truly it was frightful, the fire shooting forth afar. The mountain was on fire for a whole year, and no one could say how it could be passed. When all the warriors had arrived at its foot, no one spoke; they grieved at heart, and could not say how the fire could be captured.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 31; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then Gagavitz spoke: 'Who of you wishes that I try my fortune? He has a heart of a hero that fears not. I will go first. You must not fear so soon.' Zakitzunun wished to go with him, and together they said: 'There is no use of bows or shields.' They laid them aside, dug a trench, and placed by the water the banana trees called raxah.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 31; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then Gagavitz descended into the fire — head first, then neck, then arms, hands, and feet — while Zakitzunun conducted the water to the fire, and the green grass and maize mixed with water flowed upon it. All at the foot of the mountain fled. Gagavitz remained in the mountain, and the day drew to a close and their courage died — the fire was captured, but it was not captured for them.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 31; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then he came from within the mountain, truly terrible to see, and all the warriors said: 'Truly his power, his knowledge, his glory and his majesty are terrible. He died, and yet he has come down.' They seated him on the throne and made much of him, and he answered: 'The heart of the mountain has come as my slave, my captive.' When the heart of the mountain is opened, the fire separates from the stone — hence comes the dance called the Heart of the Mountain, danced violently with many troops.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 32; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Sacrifice of Tolgom, Son of the Mud That Quivers
title.zh: 獻祭顫泥之子托爾戈姆

region.en: Qakbatzulu, on the shore of Lake Atitlan, Guatemala
region.zh: 危地馬拉阿蒂特蘭湖畔卡克巴祖魯

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, secs. 35-38

summary.en: At trembling Qakbatzulu the migrants seize Tolgom, who calls himself 'son of the Mud that Quivers'. He is exhibited, honored as first among the warriors, then bound before a tree: as the dance begins and the arrows fly, none reach the mark until Gagavitz's own arrow leaps over Cheetzulu and pierces him. His body is divided among the seven towns, and the festival of Uchum — with children shot as his substitutes — is founded.
summary.zh: 在顫動的卡克巴祖魯，遷徙者擒獲自稱「顫泥之子」的托爾戈姆。先被展示、尊為戰士之首，後縛於樹前：舞起箭發，無一中的，直至加加維茨親自射出之箭躍過切祖魯而貫穿其身。其屍分予七鎮，烏楚姆月之祭典——以孩童中箭代之——由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: After this they arrived at the place Qakbatzulu, where they met the one named Tolgom. Truly, terror was there, and the place Qakbatzulu trembled. At first all the warriors feared lest they should meet death, and Gagavitz said: 'Who are you, oh warriors? Let us look at his face. Can we not fight?' And he sent the warriors to seize Tolgom.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 35; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then Gagavitz went to see Tolgom and cried to him: 'Who are you? You are neither my brother nor my elder. This very day I shall slay you.' And Tolgom, filled with fear, replied: 'I am the son of the Mud that Quivers. This is my house where I dwell, oh my lord.' He submitted and was made prisoner, and Gagavitz said: 'Show forth the face of my prisoner. We will adorn and sacrifice my captive, and thus celebrate the name of this spot.'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 35; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then began the execution of Tolgom. He arrayed himself and entered suddenly; his arms were extended in front of a tree, to be shot with arrows. A dance was begun by all the warriors while Tolgom began his death song; but not one of the arrows reached the cord, until the arrow of Gagavitz was discharged: it passed over the place named Cheetzulu and pierced Tolgom, and then all the arrows found him from near and from afar.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 37; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: A great stream of blood came forth behind the tree, and his body was cut in pieces and divided among all the seven towns. This gift and this sacrifice of his death founded the festival of the month Uchum, at which all were equal, with eating and drinking — and little children were shot with arrows, their heads adorned with elder flowers as his substitute, as if they were Tolgom. When they were on the hill, they threw part of the body of Tolgom into the lake, and a noise was heard in the waters, and the festival of 'Throwing the Nose of Tolgom' began.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), secs. 37-38; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: Gagavitz Becomes a White Cloud: The Lake Is Divided
title.zh: 加加維茨化白雲：湖水乃分

source.work: Annals of the Cakchiquels, trans. Daniel G. Brinton, 1885, sec. 38

summary.en: Gagavitz crosses Lake Atitlan transformed into Zutzu-Cumatz, the white crested serpent: the water darkens, a wind rises, and a white cloud circles the lake. The Tz'utujil's power must first be reduced; then the lake is halved between the two peoples, and Gagavitz remains with the Tz'utujil women while the tribes move on.
summary.zh: 加加維茨化為祖祖·庫馬茲——白冠之蛇——渡阿蒂特蘭湖：水色轉暗，風起，一朵白雲繞湖而行。先須削減祖圖希爾之力；然後湖水分半，兩族各得其一，加加維茨留於祖圖希爾的女子之中，諸族前行。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Cakchiquel annal; paraphrase of Brinton's public-domain translation.

passages.text: A little while after the arrival of Gagavitz, truly a fearful thing took place when he entered the water, having changed himself into Zutzu-Cumatz. It suddenly darkened on the water, a wind rose, and a white cloud rested on the surface, making a circuit of the water in the lake.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 38; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: They desired to remain there, but it was first necessary to reduce the power of the Tz'utuhils. All the seven nations looked about and then descended to the water, and those who were there said to the children of the Ahtziquinahay: 'We have scarcely made the circuit of this lake of ours, this sea, oh my brother. But let one half of the lake be yours, and one half of the fruits, of the wild geese, of the crabs, of the fish.' And they answered: 'It is well, my brother; half of the lake be ours, and half of thy acorns and thy bananas, and of all living things you kill in or below the waters.'
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 38; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then they separated, but soon returned, desiring to obtain wives, for none were married and no women had come with them. The Ahtziquinahay said: 'My lord, my brother, my elder, here indeed is thy maiden. You have divided with us the waters; half of the lake is thine, half is ours.' And Gagavitz said: 'I hear thy words; their victory is by the organs of their women. Remaining, I shall do this.' In this manner, say our elders, the lake was divided, and our brother and elder remained with the Tz'utuhils.
passages.note: Condensed from Brinton's translation (1885), sec. 38; not verbatim throughout.
